The trails within this network are flowing in nature with a hard-packed surface and fine grain soils. Most of the system is located on routes that climb to and traverse long and scenic ridgelines. The Wind River mountain range is visible on the western side of the system. The trails wind and meander through typical Great Basin terrain that ranges from clusters of pinyon-juniper woodlands and open sagebrush meadows. Although open year round, visitors wishing to ride on dirt rather than snow are usually restricted from mid-March to the end of November. Trails are often effectively closed during the spring thaw in early March due to extremely muddy conditions on some portions of the trail with high clay content. pages.text: Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene | National Geographic TRAVEL Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene Across the city, a growing crop of music-making events is nourishing the capital’s grassroots music scene — and helping to alleviate loneliness in the process. The Five Points Jam brings together more than 30 musicians for high-energy performances. Richard Mukuze By Sam Kemp Published November 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The jazz saxophonist Stan Getz once said that the best music sounds “like a good conversation among friends”. Right now, some of the most interesting musical conversations in London are happening at its grassroots venues, where open jam sessions are giving musicians of all levels a platform to improvise, hone their craft and form new friendships. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. London’s open jam scene really took hold in the years following the Covid lockdown — a period when music-lovers were looking for new ways to connect in a city beset by independent venue closures and the ongoing effects of social isolation. The Five Points Project, an events platform founded in 2022 by school friends James Lear and Max Riby-Williams, offered a solution: find a space, fill it with musicians and watch a community take shape. pages.text: Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand | National Geographic TRAVEL Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand A new off-grid tour takes travellers deep into New Zealand’s largest basin in search of the elusive black stilt. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. He is a graduate of the Georgetown University Law Center and the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School of Business. Mr. Brightbill clerked for the Honorable D. Brooks Smith on the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. As General Counsel, Mr. Brightbill is responsible for overseeing the legal operations of the Department of Energy, as well as counseling the Secretary, Deputy Secretary and senior leadership on the execution of their duties in the development of federal energy policy. His oversight portfolio includes nuclear energy regulatory reforms, electricity and gas markets, energy efficiency, civilian nuclear programs, business transactions, international negotiations, loan and grant investments, and oversight of the Department’s national laboratory system. Prior to joining DOE, Mr. Brightbill was a partner in the Washington, D.C. office of Winston & Strawn. pages.text: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades - BBC Sport By Richard Winton BBC Sport Scotland You know Josh Kerr, right? The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks. Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is. pages.description: The animals that plummeted 85 feet into Wyoming’s Natural Trap Cave provide a layered history of life dating back to the Pleistocene
pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. pages.description: The foresight of a primary school teacher in Wales helped to create one of the best attacking full-backs of the 1970s
pages.text: JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor | Wales rugby union team | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation JPR Williams: a rugby union great who changed full-back role – video obituary Wales rugby union team This article is more than 2 years old JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor This article is more than 2 years old Paul Rees The foresight of a primary school teacher in Wales helped to create one of the best attacking full-backs of the 1970s Tue 9 Jan 2024 12.28 EST Last modified on Wed 10 Jan 2024 05.27 EST Share J PR Williams described himself as a diehard Corinthian, but he was also a revolutionary. When he made his debut for Wales against Scotland in 1969, it was in a position then regarded as the last line of defence. Only 15 tries had been scored by full-backs in major Test matches in 88 years, but the former British junior tennis champion changed the dynamic and smoothed the way for players such as Andy Irvine, Serge Blanco and John Gallagher. Williams, who qualified as an orthopaedic surgeon while playing for London Welsh, scored six tries in his 55 internationals for Wales, five against England, an opponent he boasted a 100% success rate against in 11 Tests. He was qualified to wear the white jersey as his mother, Margaret, was born in Rochdale, but there was never the remotest chance of a boy born and raised in the Bridgend area turning his back on his homeland. pages.text: Juan Mata: Former Spain midfielder retires aged 38 - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Mata celebrates winning Euro 2012 with Spain Published 18 November 2026 Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38. Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy. A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup. Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022. He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory. "Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development. "I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer." Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals. "What a player," Chelsea posted on social media. Laferte began the concert solo with the torch song "Pa' Dónde Se Fue" (Where Did You Go?). She sang the break-up story with a smirk that belied the heartache hiding in her poignant lyrics. Then, after a short set break starring the Tiny Desk engineer Josh Rogosin, Juanes joined her to perform the duo's sultry single, "Amárrame" (Tie Me Up). It's rare to see Juanes in such an intimate setting. After almost two decades of performing solo, the Latin pop star is more of a stadium and arena kind of guy. This marked a return to the intimacy that fueled his earliest days and that's still present in the personal lyrics that have sold millions of records. That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. pages.text: Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Skip Navigation Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) May 01, 2024 The Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) is a Census Bureau experimental data product that measures the economic and health outcomes of people who have been involved with the criminal justice system. Criminal justice involvement can include criminal charges, prison releases, and probation and parole sentences. Outcomes measured include employment, earnings, government program participation, and mortality. JOE is a collaboration between the U.S. Census Bureau and the University of Michigan that uses Criminal Justice Administrative Records System (CJARS) data to better understand how people involved in the justice system reintegrate into society. JOE covers criminal justice system involvement at any point between 2000 and 2020. Actual coverage of justice involvement depends on the coverage of agencies in the CJARS data, while coverage of outcomes depends on the availability of source data at the Census Bureau. Data users can download JOE data below or interact directly with the JOE data using the data visualization tool hosted by the University of Michigan. The tool includes additional justice-related outcomes created from CJARS without Census Bureau data. Justin Bis Justin Bis is the Chief of Staff for the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) at the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he works alongside OTC leadership to maximize the impact of DOE’s investments in technology commercialization, strengthen coordination across the agency, and ensure long-term success. Mr. Bis has more than a decade of experience in government service and public life. He previously served at the White House as Special Assistant to President Trump and Deputy Director of the Presidential Personnel Office, where he managed the appointment of senior government officials responsible for regulating the U.S. financial and energy markets. At DOE, he was the Director of Intergovernmental and External Affairs under Secretary Dan Brouillette, serving as the department’s primary liaison to trade associations, labor unions, and state, local, and tribal governments. Beyond his federal service, Mr. Bis was the Executive Director of the Ohio Republican Party and Ohio Deputy State Director for the Donald J. Trump for President campaign. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Northern Michigan University.

pages.description: Usman Khawaja's autobiography has exposed the limbo Australian cricket finds itself stuck in over the sandpaper scandal, writes Stephan Shemilt.
pages.text: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 10 November 2026 There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements. Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another. Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins? Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018. Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years. It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot. Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation. Like any balance, it is designed to equalize one force with another: In this case, the weight of a test mass is exactly offset by a force produced when an electrical current is run through a coil of wire immersed in a surrounding magnetic field. The surrounding field is provided by a large permanent magnet system or an electromagnet. The moveable coil, once electrified, becomes an electromagnet with a field strength proportional to the amount of current it conducts. When the coil's field interacts with the surrounding magnetic field, an upward force is exerted on the coil. The magnitude of that force is controlled by adjusting the current. The field office is also home to the historic Route 66 Back Country Byway , as well as the largest wild burro population in the country, located in the Black Mountains. Resources include portions of the Sonoran, Mohave, and Great Basin deserts, with saguaro cactus, greasewood, Joshua tree, sagebrush, chaparral, pinyon-juniper woodlands, and ponderosa pine forests. The field office manages nine wilderness areas, 12 Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, and five river segments under consideration for Wild and Scenic River designations. Medio millón de caribúes lo atraviesan en su migración, y sus pisadas se entrecruzan en las dunas esculpidas. El río Kobuk es una vía antigua y actual para el hombre y la fauna. Durante 9,000 años, la gente vino a Onion Portage para atrapar caribúes mientras cruzaban el río. Esta tradición continúa aun hoy en día. Las dunas de Great Kobuk se encuentran a 40 millas (64 km) por encima del círculo ártico; no obstante, ¡la temperatura de verano puede alcanzar los 100 °F (38 °C)! Una de las verdaderas rarezas de Alaska es que, en algunos lugares, la arena puede alcanzar los 100 pies (30 m) de altura.
